Early Indicator Shows Strong Effect of AI on Job Prospects of Entry-Level Workers | Press release | ifo Institute

9 November 2026 

# Early Indicator Shows Strong Effect of AI on Job Prospects of Entry-Level Workers

The use of artificial intelligence (AI) is changing the labor market, above all for young job seekers. This is suggested by a new early indicator from the ifo Institute that tracks the effects of AI on the labor market. Employment of young people starting their careers is falling in occupations with high exposure to AI, while overall employment remains stable. “We see no sign so far of broad job losses due to AI. But those starting out in working life are the first to feel the change,” says ifo President Clemens Fuest.

The indicator compares employment and hiring by age across 140 occupations and relates them to the AI exposure of the tasks involved. In the most exposed occupations, employment has grown by 1.8 percent since the third quarter of 2022, while in the least exposed it has fallen by 6.4 percent. By contrast, full-time employment among 20- to 24-year-olds in the most exposed occupations fell by 14 percent, from around 279,000 to 239,000. “Starting a career is the labor market’s early warning system. This is where we should observe the consequences of AI, long before they become visible in productivity growth,” says Oliver Falck, Director of the ifo Center for the Economics of Innovation and Digital Transformation.

According to the ifo experts, what matters is how AI is used. “Whether AI complements or automates tasks makes the difference for those starting out. In areas such as clerical support work or IT support, which have so far offered good entry opportunities, AI can already take over many tasks,” says ifo economist Yuchen Guo. The indicator also offers pointers for the European Union: where AI mainly automates, young employees are hired less often than older ones. The authors stress, however, that while the indicator describes a development, it cannot be used to infer that the increased use of AI alone is behind it. What influence demographic change, longer training periods, or more difficult onboarding under remote work have remains to be examined. It is therefore advisable to keep monitoring hiring by age and occupational group on an ongoing, differentiated basis, taking the latest AI technologies into account as well. In any case, the ifo researchers consider it necessary to align the training of workers more closely with skills that complement AI.
